notes: The French corpus comes out of the right-hand column of the same document as the English one. Before the columns were separated, this corpus did not exist at all: both language rows pointed at one URL, so only English was ingested.
expect_text pins French sentences whose English translation sits immediately to their left. A regression in the gutter split puts that English into these chunks.
French definitions carry no defining verb - « pavillon-jardin » Logement supplémentaire ... - so they are recognised by guillemets and a capitalised body rather than by a word like 'means'.

questions.question: Qu'est-ce qu'un pavillon-jardin?
questions.why: The verbless French definition form. Nothing matched it until the guillemets were treated as the marker.

questions.question: Est-ce qu'un pavillon-jardin peut être dans un bâtiment accessoire?
questions.why: Pairs with garden-suite-count in the English set: the same provision, retrieved in the language it was asked in.

questions.question: Puis-je élever des poules dans ma cour arrière?
questions.why: Urban agriculture in French. The English translation of this clause sits on the same physical lines.

questions.question: Ai-je le droit d'abattre des poules sur mon terrain?
questions.why: A one-sentence provision. If the columns bleed, this chunk carries its English twin.

questions.question: Quelles sont les normes applicables aux lots dans les zones rurales?
questions.why: This page mixes two-column prose above a full-width table, and was interleaving both languages until lines were classified individually. The table is part of section 158 rather than a clause of its own: its page carries prose too, so it joins the clause flow. expect_text therefore pins the zone codes, which is what the table is for.
